extracted.intended_audience: researchers and stakeholders in behavioral/social science (authors, editors, funders) interested in adversarial collaborations and research-reform practices
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and normative guidance on designing, conducting, and promoting adversarial collaborations (ACs) — projects where researchers with opposing views cooperate to empirically test contested claims. Covers benefits, necessary practices (e.g., registered reports), participant selection, and institutional incentives/obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of adversarial collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers who have very different views about some phenomena, and often have publicly staked out very different positions, working together to empirically resolve some, or maybe all, of those differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames ACs as explicit joint empirical efforts to resolve disagreements. Use this definition to decide whether a project qualifies as an AC versus ordinary collaboration or debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use high-quality, high-rigor methods to falsify opponents' hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea is that adversaries can hold each others’ feet to the fire to ensure that high quality, high rigor methods are used to provide the strongest possible methods to falsify each other's pet theories and hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tests that are severe and capable of falsifying claims rather than 'softball tests' that favor one side. Prioritize methodological choices that directly address the competing claims and minimize biased choices of measures, samples, or analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value claims that 'pass' severe tests as more credible
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there is no guarantee, a claim that passes such 'severe tests' should usually be more credible than claims subjected to softball tests built on researchers’ preferences or unintentional biases in favor of their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating evidence from ACs, give greater weight to findings that survived pre-specified, stringent tests agreed upon by adversaries. Treat outcomes from ad-hoc or post-hoc-favored tests with more skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine ACs with Registered Reports (RR) and Registered Replication Reports (RRR)
rubrics_metrics.description: RRs and RRRs work well with ACs. ACs can help ensure that RRs and RRRs truly are the fairest and most rigorous tests of the hypotheses they purport to test. And RRs help lock adversaries into an explicit research plan to avoid post hoc quibbling about a priori predictions. RRRs are almost inevitably adversarial in that they challenge an earlier finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-register the design, hypotheses, analyses, and sample sizes (use RRs/RRRs where possible) so adversaries are committed to the plan. This reduces post-hoc disputes and increases credibility of outcomes. Expect journals and editors to play a facilitating role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors/publishers should require critics and targets to make good-faith efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be easy for journal editors to require critics of the published work of others—and the targets of such critiques—to make a good-faith effort to explore differences constructively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for editorial policies that compel or incentivize structured engagement (e.g., joint replications, invited adversarial responses) rather than endless point-scoring commentary. Use this as a mechanism to institutionalize ACs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select participants who are curious, credible, and not primarily defending honor
rubrics_metrics.description: They seem to work best when involving people who like each other, but have different views on a topic but are legitimately curious if they are right and think it’s cool if they aren’t rather than being in some kind of position to defend their honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer collaborators with reputations for integrity, openness, and methodological competence (not those grinding political or careerist axes). Avoid pairing participants who are primarily motivated by public point-scoring or reputational defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and plan for practical obstacles (hostility, time, fear of humiliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: These projects are hard... In many of these areas scholars have often worked hard to destroy each other. The idea they’d then want to blow several years of precious life with the constant stress of working together is fantasy. You could 'force' them, but I’m not sure that’s quite right. Much of the culture in academic publishing right now involves the fear of humiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic: ACs take time, emotional labor, and risk. Build protections (clear authorship agreements, conflict resolution procedures), allow for long timelines, and recognize that not all disputes are practically solvable via ACs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require cultural and incentive changes to scale ACs
rubrics_metrics.description: To expedite adoption of ACs, those who control incentives in science (publishers, employers, editors, funders, etc.) should reward and encourage ACs from scholars who publish conclusions that contradict other conclusions. My hope is that over time, ACs could change the culture of science to one where scientific disagreements are resolved faster and more cordially, and belief updating is embraced as a normal and desirable part of the scientific process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should create rewards (funding, recognition, publication pathways) and reduce penalties for null results or being 'wrong' to make ACs feasible at scale. Without incentive change, uptake will be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACs are best-suited for empirical questions, not all disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no 'study' that can be performed to 'show' that Stalin and Castro were... left extremists... Some disputes are not amenable to empirical resolution; ACs are for empirical disagreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before launching an AC, assess whether the disagreement is an empirical question addressable by data and agreed-upon operationalizations. Avoid deploying AC methods for purely conceptual, definitional, or normative disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use larger samples, open data/materials, pre-registration, and report effect sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many improvements... such as open data and materials, pre-registration and registered reports, larger samples, reporting of effect sizes along with p-values, etc. started with reformers... ACs can help ensure these practices are followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt open-science best practices within ACs: adequate sample sizes, transparent materials, data sharing, and emphasis on effect sizes to improve reproducibility and reduce post-hoc disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect limited immediate cultural impact and plan communication accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: I doubt it will change the minds of the many true-believers... You keep banging your head against the wall and, mostly, you just get a headache. But once in a while, eventually... you never know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ACs as long-term investments. Plan dissemination with realistic expectations: journals may ignore failed replications, and entrenched beliefs may persist despite strong evidence. Consider multiple communication channels and replication chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lock in explicit research plans to avoid post-hoc quibbling
rubrics_metrics.description: RRs help lock adversaries into an explicit research plan to avoid post hoc quibbling about a priori predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly document agreed hypotheses, decision rules, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and analysis pipelines before data collection. Use pre-registration or in-principle acceptance to make deviations transparent and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACs often function as Registered Replication Reports (RRRs) for contested findings
rubrics_metrics.description: RRRs are almost inevitably adversarial in that they challenge an earlier finding, so AC approaches would almost always be appropriate for RRRs (assuming advocates of the findings in question are still active researchers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting replications of influential or contested findings, use adversarial designs where proponents and skeptics co-design the replication to ensure fair tests and mutual buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer adversaries with demonstrable methodological competence rather than political motives
rubrics_metrics.description: I knew he was a hardcore quant/data type and saw no evidence of him grinding political axes in any of his (extensive) prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prior work for methodological rigor and apparent absence of partisan signaling. This reduces risks that ACs devolve into partisan theater rather than rigorous tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for multi-study, multi-year projects when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: This replication was a registered replication report ... including much larger sample sizes, and submitted... we followed their methods almost to the letter... After being rejected by PNAS... it was given a provisional acceptance... Unless they judge we screwed up bigtime, they will publish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect some ACs (especially replications of high-impact findings) to require multiple studies, large samples, and extended editorial negotiation; budget time and resources accordingly.
